title: An Exact Method for the Minimum Feedback Arc Set Problem
contribution: An exact MFAS method that generates cycle rows lazily inside Gurobi, chosen by a greedy repair heuristic and BFS shortest cycles, plus a public 4,468-graph benchmark with optima and clearly evaluated limits.
problem_entry: Application entry (tearing in chemical-process flowsheeting); set-cover formulation fails because sparse graphs can have exponentially many simple cycles; question put as practical limits of an exact method on sparse graphs (pp. 1-6, 8, 16).
key_idea: Lazy cycle generation: solve set-cover relaxation, certify by topological sort, else heuristic feedback arc set gives incumbent and seeds BFS shortest cycles as new rows; novelty in how rows are chosen (pp. 8-11).
assumptions: Directed simple graphs, nonnegative weights, pure-binary set-cover IP; target class sparse graphs; finite termination by row growth; BFS row choice may fail on pathological weights (pp. 2-3, 7, 9, 11, 16, 21-22).
proof_devices: termination by cycle-matrix growth of at least one row per iteration (p. 9)
lazy constraints in MIPSOL callback vs cuts in MIPNODE callback (p. 11)
SCC splitting and run/bypass removal presolve (p. 12)
safe-arc-removal rule c1 = c2 with fake nodes u, v (pp. 18-22)
experiments: 11 chemical graphs with published optima, 3,737 Erdős–Rényi, 24 de Bruijn/Imase–Itoh, 707 tournaments, complete graph n=30; baseline triangle IP in same Gurobi; medians over 101 graphs per point, no seeds; losses printed (tournaments n>=32, one time-out under Gurobi 8.1.0, unsolved counts) (pp. 12-18).
positioning: Reviews DP, custom B&B and IP exact methods; triangle formulation and Grötschel–Jünger–Reinelt cutting planes classed as dense-graph methods; hedged novelty for lazy constraint generation in MFAS (pp. 7-8, 11).
writing: Numbered contributions in conclusion, hedged abstract, scope fences, worst-case experiments announced as such, negative experiment reported plainly (pp. 1, 8, 11, 12, 17).
limits_future: Built for sparse graphs; possible BFS failure on pathological weights; safe-removal too costly for presolve; unhandled corner case; Python presolve weak; future: better shortest-path routine, sparse-graph cutting planes left to others (pp. 8-9, 11-13, 17-18, 22).

method_links.note: Co-signed. Correctness cross-checked on graphs with published optima against both IP formulations before scaling; easy graphs kept for cross-checking; optima published with graphs; check on final optima, not derived objects.

Problem-specific, so no detector and no no-op path; the class it was not built for (tournaments, complete graph) is run on purpose and the loss printed: worst-case safeguard done as a test, not a gate.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The repair heuristic's feedback arc set is both the incumbent and the seed of the next lazy rows.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: correctness rows lazily, the host solver's cuts kept
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Add only what an incomplete model needs for correctness and leave performance cuts to the commercial solver; stated as the reason not to compete with its cutting planes (Quote 1).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: scalability-grid benchmark with a deliberate worst-case family
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Generator families over size and density, 101 instances per point, easy points kept, one family the method is not built for.

transferable: [D2] Use the repair heuristic's output twice. It is the incumbent, and each of its arcs seeds a BFS shortest cycle that becomes a new lazy row (pp. 9–11).
[D4] Put the constraints needed for correctness in a lazy (MIPSOL) callback and leave performance cuts to the host solver. Say in the paper which is which (p. 11).
[D4] Certify a relaxation solution with a linear-time combinatorial check (topological sort) instead of the full constraint set (p. 9).

[D4] Safe-reduction test: if the exact cost of the induced subproblem equals a heuristic's cost of also breaking every boundary cycle, the heuristic's arcs are safe to fix. Fake source and sink nodes expose the boundary cycles (pp. 19–22).
[D5] Build the benchmark as a grid over size and density: 101 instances per point, medians, easy points kept, and one family outside the design class (pp. 12–17).
[D5] State a method's limit as "k of 101 unsolved within T at size n", not as a single average (pp. 17–18).
[D5] When the solver version changes during a revision, rerun the hardest set and report what changed (p. 15).
coauthors: Ali Baharev, Hermann Schichl, Arnold Neumaier

quotes.text: Any research attempting to implement a novel cutting plane algorithm has to compete with that strong baseline.

title: MIPLIB 2017: data-driven compilation of the 6th mixed-integer programming library
contribution: The MIPLIB 2017 collection (1,065 instances) and benchmark set (240) selected by a fully data-driven, optimization-based methodology of features, clusterings and selection MIPs.
problem_entry: Measured progress made MIPLIB 2010 no longer frontier (virtual best 36.3 s to 13.5 s, open instances 134 to 70); 5,721 candidates and a multi-solver committee called for a fair, transparent selection (pp. 2-3, 7, 24).
key_idea: Selection as a sequence of MIPs: 105 features after trivial presolve, max-min diversity preselection, k-means per feature group, collection MIP with balancedness and caps, benchmark MIP with performance clusterings and runtime budget (pp. 12-14, 26-36).
assumptions: Definition 1 canonical MIP with normalised rows; indicator constraints allowed in collection only; benchmark suitability criteria B.1-B.9 with exclusion counts; unbounded instances dropped (pp. 13-14, 17-18, 25-26).
proof_devices: diversity preselection MIP (1) with linearised products (pp. 26-27)
clustering quality and L_k threshold of 90% (pp. 29-30)
balancedness constraints with epsilon = 0.5 and epsilon-sensitivity table (pp. 29-33)
performance clusterings: absolute ranks, shifted relative ratio, binned times (pp. 33-35)
benchmark MIP (8) with 32-day budget and hardness weight (pp. 35-36)
exact-arithmetic solution checker with scaled tolerance (pp. 22-23)
experiments: Eight solvers, 4 h limit, ~40 CPU years, reported only as virtual best/median/worst; Table 11 new vs old benchmark; feature space recovers model groups; one-sided KS tests per solver; variability not captured, no seeds (pp. 20-23, 36-41).
positioning: MIPLIB lineage from 1992; reporting standards of Crowder–Dembo–Mulvey and Jackson et al.; extension of Hooker 1993; instance-space analysis called complementary; earlier manual selections credited (pp. 2-6).
writing: Transparency motivates detail; use limit stated first; manual decisions listed upfront; outcome called one of many; computing details and corrections in footnotes (pp. 2-4, 16, 42-44).
limits_future: Not a general blueprint; snapshot without variability; favours tractable instances; numerically problematic instances slipped through (June 2019 update); future: judge representability in hindsight via model-group speed-ups (pp. 36, 43-44).

method_links.note: Co-signed, for its statistics: shifted geometric mean with shift 1 s credited to Achterberg's thesis; shifted ratio ranks solvers; time-outs scored at 4 h limit; exponential time bins and the >= 10 s floor in B.2. Step 7: paper states performance variability was not captured, consistent with Misreading 1 (no seeds).

Test-set choice separated from any one code: eight solvers' data, criteria with exclusion counts; exact-arithmetic solution checker and cross-solver consistency check, inconsistent instances excluded and counted (Workflow C checkpoint applied to library building).

For its two-set rule and stated Limitation: average benchmark performance does not tell which solver suits an application class, so a class-specific claim needs the class's own set beside the general one (step 4).

[D3] Write benchmark suitability as numbered criteria and print how many instances each one removed (pp. 25–26).

title: Efficient Separation of RLT Cuts for Implicit and Explicit Bilinear Products
contribution: Detection of implicit bilinear products in MILPs plus row marking and projection filtering that make RLT cut separation efficient, implemented in SCIP and Gurobi 10.0 beta.
problem_entry: RLT gives strong relaxations at the cost of excessive cuts; RLT not applied to hidden bilinear relations in MILPs, and separation cost is the major bottleneck (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Detect implicit products from pairs of linear constraints (Theorem 1), mark rows LT/GT/BOTH by violation sign, and test projected violation before building the full cut (pp. 5-10).
assumptions: MI(N)LP with bilinear relations, finite bounds; detection needs x_i binary, b1b2 > 0, gamma != 0, plus practical filters; projection assumes McCormick holds at x*; test sets keep only instances with products (pp. 4-7, 9-10).
proof_devices: Theorem 1 by coefficient matching with scaling parameters alpha, beta (p. 6)
row-marking data structures row_idcs/row_marks and sparse W (pp. 8-9)
separator budgets: 20 terms, every 10 nodes, 1/10 rounds (p. 10)
experiments: SCIP on MINLPLib (1,357) and 195 MILPs, 1 h, shifted geomeans (1 s, 100 nodes), affected and bracket rows, all-optimal subset; Gurobi 10.0 beta on internal 5,011 MILP / 806 MINLP set; separation share tables; losses printed in body; no seeds stated though counts ~5x test sets; table/text inconsistencies (pp. 10-14).
positioning: RLT lineage (Adams–Sherali, Sherali–Tuncbilek, reduced RLT), McCormick; contrast to multiplication-only approaches; baseline only the standard separation algorithm (pp. 3-5, 7).
writing: Two contributions announced; neutral abstract; slowdowns stated in body but Summary mentions only gains; cross-solver caution; inconsistencies suggest fast turnaround (inferred) (pp. 3-4, 11, 14-15).
limits_future: No limitations or future-work section; open points: implicit products cost time on MINLPs, SCIP MILP gain only from 100 s bracket, separation share still 100% on some MINLPs (pp. 11-13, 15).

method_links.note: Co-signed. Off vs on in the full solver, brackets [x, timelim], affected instances by LP iterations, shifts stated (1 s, 100 nodes), all-optimal subset; same bracket rows for SCIP and Gurobi. Lacks counts of models >= 10% faster/slower (step 4), Gurobi table omits its shift.
Step 7 and Misreading 1: no seeds or permutations stated, but counts ~5x test sets and D023 mentions permuted instances; if confirmed, Misreading 1 needs a qualifier for co-signed work from 2022 on.

Nodes down and time up reported; root-bound gain printed beside time loss; separator time share measured and cut 54.2% to 2.8% (step 2); budget in solver-internal units (step 4); node increase traced to censoring via all-optimal subset.

Step 1 detector on the matrix and step 5 two-code check appear, but SCIP set keeps only instances where the component acts, no default decision stated; MILP case split: no slowdown in Gurobi, 3% slower overall in SCIP.
Global-optimization technique (RLT, McCormick) enters MILP through a structure detector and new data structures, each piece tested alone; not a SAT/CP import, novelty placed against RLT literature.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Mark rows by the sign of each term's violation contribution before building any cut.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: cheap projected violation check before building the full cut
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Works because a basic LP solution puts many variables at bounds.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: all-optimal subset to tell censoring from search effects
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Faster code explores more nodes before the time limit, so check node ratios where every setting finishes.

transferable: [D4] Derive a hidden bilinear relation from two linear constraints in (x_i binary, x_j, w_ij). Require b1b2 > 0, γ ≠ 0 and opposite signs on x_i's coefficients (pp. 6–7).
[D4] Before separating products of rows and bound factors, mark each row by the sign of its terms' violation contributions, and build only the row × factor pairs that can be violated (pp. 7–9).
[D4] Test violation on the system projected onto the non-bound variables first, and build the full cut only on success (pp. 9–10).
[D4] Budget a separator by call frequency (every 10 nodes), rounds (10 at the root, 1 elsewhere) and a cap on new product terms per cut (20) (p. 10).
[D5] Report a separator's share of total time per setting: its mean, its maximum, a histogram over share bands, and failures (Table 6, p. 13).
[D5] When a faster component raises node counts, check the all-optimal subset to separate censoring from changes in the search (p. 13).
[D5] Run one algorithm in an open and in a commercial solver. Report the same bracket table for both and claim only the shared tendencies (pp. 11, 14).
